analysis.one_liner: Requires all derivatives and swaps to be traded on regulated exchanges instead of unregulated private deals.
analysis.headline: The bill never attracted a single cosponsor and died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the legal exemptions that since 2000 let big banks and other dealers trade swaps and other derivatives privately, outside the view of regulators. Every commodity agreement, contract, and transaction would have had to happen on a regulated exchange overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, where prices are public and rules against manipulation apply. It was introduced just over a year after the financial crisis, when unregulated credit-default swaps were widely seen as a central cause of the meltdown.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, in two ways. First, the 2008 crisis showed that unregulated derivatives could take down financial institutions and take the wider economy down with them; exchange trading with public prices, margin rules, and anti-manipulation enforcement reduces that risk. Second, speculators trading commodity derivatives off-exchange were widely blamed for violent swings in food and energy prices; a public exchange makes those markets harder to corner. It would also have benefited regulated futures exchanges, which would have gained the trading volume that previously stayed in private dealer markets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary households exposed to financial crashes and price swings

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the exemptions in the Commodity Exchange Act (including the ones created by the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000) that let swaps and other derivative transactions escape Commodity Futures Trading Commission regulation entirely.

Requires futures and derivatives trading to occur only on regulated contract markets or derivatives transaction execution facilities, and abolishes exempt boards of trade, so transactions happen where prices are public and rules apply.
The stated purpose is to ensure that all agreements, contracts, and transactions with respect to commodities are carried out on a regulated exchange.

analysis.who_pays: Large banks and swap dealers, which had built a profitable multi-trillion-dollar over-the-counter derivatives business behind the legal exemptions this bill repeals. They would lose market-making profits, the ability to price deals privately with individual customers, and the freedom to trade without margin or position limits. Companies that used customized over-the-counter swaps to hedge business risks — airlines hedging fuel, farmers and food processors hedging crops, energy producers — would have to move that hedging onto exchanges, likely paying more and getting less tailored contracts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big banks and swap dealers, plus firms hedging with custom swaps

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates every over-the-counter exemption at once, including ones commercial end-users used to hedge real business risks with customized contracts. Firms would have to fit their hedges into standardized exchange products, which could cost more and fit worse. [S3]
A one-size-fits-all mandate to trade everything on a domestic regulated exchange could push derivatives trading to foreign venues with weaker rules, rather than subjecting it to regulation here. [S3]

The bill was drafted as a clean repeal with no transition provisions, so it offered no phase-in for a market of this size — a real cost an honest supporter would have had to address in committee. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: exchange trading sacrifices the customization and dealer profits of the private market in exchange for public prices, margin, and anti-manipulation rules, after unregulated swaps helped cause a crisis that cost millions of people jobs, homes, and savings. The bill's weakness is design, not aim — it bans the exemptions wholesale with no phase-in and no tailored carve-out for genuine commercial hedging, which is why even friendly committees had a reason to rewrite rather than advance it. Better-built versions of the same idea were debated in the years that followed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in January 2009, got zero cosponsors, and the committee never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Harkin introduced the bill on January 15, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. [S5]
No cosponsors joined from either party. [S4]
The action history records nothing after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired with the 111th Congress. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The banks and dealers whose over-the-counter derivatives business the bill would have shut down kept that market operating under the old exemptions for another two years; even the watered-down derivatives regulation that eventually passed in 2010 left substantial parts of the dealer market outside exchanges. Commercial end-users that liked customized private hedges also kept the status quo. Ordinary people got the riskiest features of that market regulated only partially and years later.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unregulated swap dealers kept their market another two years

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks; no other senator joined him.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; took no action
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, reported the bill out, or scheduled it for floor consideration.

against.name: Wall Street banks and swap dealers
against.role: Firms profiting from unregulated over-the-counter derivatives
against.what_they_did: Opposed proposals to move derivatives onto regulated exchanges; none supported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, so no roll call exists; the only signal is that its sole sponsor was a Democrat and zero senators of either party cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Wall Street banks and over-the-counter swap dealers
industries.note: The bill repeals the exemptions that let these firms trade swaps privately outside CFTC oversight, ending a highly profitable unregulated business. Its gain came at the cost of transparency and safety for everyone exposed to the financial system, which is everyone. [S2, S3]

industries.industry: Commercial hedgers (airlines, farmers, food and energy companies)
industries.note: Firms that used customized over-the-counter swaps to hedge real business risks would have to move onto standardized exchange contracts, likely at higher cost. Some were also the counterparties dealers profited from, and their preference for private deals was part of what the bill targeted. [S3]

Trading that previously stayed in private dealer markets would have been routed onto regulated contract markets, giving exchanges the volume. Because those exchanges operate under public-price and anti-manipulation rules, their gain lines up with the bill's public purpose. [S3]
